client: I just got my final project grade back and it was way lower than I expected. Now I can't stop thinking that maybe I'm not cut out for this program after all. I'm not sure talking about it will help - the grade is already set, so what's the point?
therapist: I hear how disappointing and discouraging this grade feels for you, and it makes sense that it's making you question your place in the program. While we can't change the grade, we can explore how this experience is affecting your thoughts and confidence—would you be open to looking at what this situation means to you?

client: I just feel like this grade proves I don't belong here. Everyone else seems to get it so easily while I'm struggling to keep up. I know we're supposed to look at my thoughts about it, but right now it just feels like the truth - maybe I'm not cut out for this program.
therapist: It sounds like this grade has reinforced some deep doubts about your abilities, and I can hear how painful that is for you. When you say "everyone else seems to get it easily," I wonder if we might explore whether that's the full picture—what makes you feel others aren't struggling too?

client:
I don't know... when I see people in class asking questions or discussing the material, they just seem so confident. Meanwhile I'm sitting there feeling completely lost. It's like they're all speaking a different language that I never learned. 

But I guess maybe some people are just better at hiding their struggles? I still feel like I'm the only one who has to work this hard just to keep up. It makes me wonder if I'm just not cut out for this program.
therapist: You're recognizing that appearances can be deceiving, and that's an important insight—it takes courage to acknowledge that others might be masking their struggles too. I wonder what it would feel like to consider that working hard to understand something doesn't mean you don't belong, but rather that you're deeply engaging with the material?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to shake this feeling that everyone else just "gets it" naturally while I have to work twice as hard. Even if they're struggling too, they seem to handle it better - like they belong here and I don't. 

When you say I'm deeply engaging with the material, it sounds nice in theory, but in the moment all I feel is frustration and this sinking sense that I'm falling behind.
therapist: I hear how real and heavy that frustration feels in the moment, and how it overshadows the perspective that you're actually putting in meaningful work. What would it be like to consider that this sense of falling behind might be more about your expectations of yourself than your actual progress?

client:
I get what you're saying about expectations, but it's hard not to feel like I'm failing when I see other people my age accomplishing so much. The anxiety just takes over and makes it feel like I'll never catch up, no matter how hard I try. 

Part of me knows I'm being too hard on myself, but another part thinks maybe I should be pushing myself even harder. It's this constant back-and-forth in my head that's exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two very demanding voices—one that says you're failing and another that says you should push harder—and that tension feels exhausting to carry. I wonder if we could explore what "catching up" would realistically look like for you, rather than comparing to others' paths?

client: I guess I know logically that comparing myself to others isn't helpful, but it's hard to stop. When I see friends hitting milestones like promotions or relationships, my brain automatically goes "you're behind" and then "you need to work twice as hard." The idea of defining my own version of success feels... vague and unsatisfying somehow. Like I'm just making excuses for not being where I "should" be.
therapist: That "should" carries so much weight, doesn't it? It's interesting how even when we recognize that comparisons aren't helpful, there's still this powerful emotional pull toward them. What do you think it would take for your own version of success to feel just as valid—not as an excuse, but as a genuine path forward?

client: It’s hard to feel like my version of success is valid when everyone around me seems to be achieving so much more. Even if I tell myself not to compare, it feels like I’m falling behind, and that “should” keeps creeping in—like I *should* be doing better by now. I guess I’m just not sure how to let go of that pressure and focus on what actually matters to me.
therapist: It makes complete sense that letting go of comparison feels nearly impossible when those "shoulds" are reinforced by what you see around you every day. I wonder—when you think about moments you've felt genuinely proud of yourself, what was different about how you measured your progress then?

client:
Hmm, I can think of a few times I felt proud, but they seem so small compared to what everyone else is achieving. Like when I finally went to the gym three times in a week, but then I see influencers posting about their six-pack abs and I just feel ridiculous. It's like my accomplishments don't count unless they're Instagram-worthy. 

Even when I try to focus on my own progress, I keep hearing this voice saying "but look how much better everyone else is doing." It makes me not want to bother trying at all.
therapist: It sounds like that critical voice immediately diminishes your accomplishments by holding them up against impossible standards—as if something only "counts" if it's extraordinary by external measures. What would it feel like to acknowledge that your three gym visits were meaningful progress *for you*, regardless of what anyone else is doing?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to feel like three gym visits matter when I see people online who go every single day without fail. It makes my effort seem so small in comparison. Even though I know I shouldn't compare myself, I can't help feeling like I'm already falling behind.
therapist: It's understandable that seeing others' consistency makes your own efforts feel insignificant—comparison can shrink even meaningful progress down to nothing. I wonder if we could explore what "falling behind" actually means in this context, since fitness isn't a race with a finish line?

client:
I get what you're saying about it not being a race, but it's hard not to feel like I'm losing when I see my friends hitting new personal records every week. I've been stuck at the same weight for months now, and it makes me feel like I'm doing something wrong even though I'm trying my best. 

The whole "don't compare yourself" advice sounds nice in theory, but how do I actually stop feeling this way when the evidence is right there in front of me?
therapist: I hear how frustrating it is to feel stuck while seeing others progress—it makes your efforts feel invisible and can really drain your motivation. What if we looked at this differently: could "evidence" also include the fact that you've maintained consistency despite not seeing changes, which is actually a significant achievement in itself?
